    map.put(k,v);
}

This check-then-act sequence is not atomic.

Use:

map.putIfAbsent(k,v);

or

map.computeIfAbsent(...)

instead.

❌ Storing null values

map.put("A",null);

Results in

NullPointerException

because ConcurrentHashMap prohibits null keys and values.

❌ Assuming iteration is a snapshot

Iterators are weakly consistent, not immutable snapshots.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
✅ Prefer computeIfAbsent() over manual check-then-put logic.

✅ Use merge() for concurrent counters.

✅ Use immutable value objects whenever possible.

✅ Avoid long-running work inside computeIfAbsent() mapping functions.

✅ Remember that ConcurrentHashMap is thread-safe within a single JVM, not across multiple application instances.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:

  • Java 7 used segment-based locking; Java 8 moved to bucket-level synchronization.
  • Reads are generally lock-free.
  • CAS reduces lock contention.
  • computeIfAbsent(), putIfAbsent(), and merge() provide atomic operations.
  • Weakly consistent iterators allow safe iteration during concurrent modifications.
  • It is the preferred choice for thread-safe in-memory maps in enterprise Java applications.

It is one of the most elegant concurrent collections in Java and is frequently used in event listeners, observer patterns, Spring Framework internals, and configuration registries.

docs.title: Q1. Why is it called Copy-On-Write?
docs.text: Because every write operation creates a new copy of the underlying array before applying the modification.

docs.title: Q2. Why are reads so fast?
docs.text: Readers access the current array directly without locking or copying.

docs.title: Q3. Why doesn't it throw ConcurrentModificationException?
docs.text: Its iterators work on a snapshot of the array rather than the live collection.

docs.title: Q4. Is it suitable for write-heavy applications?
docs.text:

docs.title: Q5. What is the biggest disadvantage?
docs.text: Every write creates a new array, increasing memory allocation and garbage collection overhead.

docs.title: Production Scenario
docs.text:
Interviewer:

"Your application has thousands of event listeners reading a shared list, but new listeners are registered only a few times each day. Which collection would you choose?"

  • Snapshot iterators avoid ConcurrentModificationException.
  • The low write frequency makes the copying overhead acceptable.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
✅ Use for read-mostly workloads.

✅ Use snapshot iterators when concurrent modification is expected.

✅ Prefer immutable objects inside the list where practical.

docs.title: Common Mistakes

❌ Ignoring the memory overhead of copying large arrays.

❌ Assuming iterators always reflect the latest changes-they reflect the state of the list when the iterator was created.

docs.title: Chapter 15 - BlockingQueue (The Producer-Consumer Pattern)
docs.text:
"One of the biggest challenges in concurrent programming is coordinating work between threads. Producers generate tasks, consumers process them. BlockingQueue provides a safe, efficient, and elegant way to connect the two."

BlockingQueue is the backbone of many enterprise systems, including ThreadPoolExecutor, Kafka consumers, asynchronous order processing, logging frameworks, messaging systems, and batch processing pipelines.

docs.title: 15.1 Why Do We Need BlockingQueue?
docs.text:
Imagine an e-commerce application.

Orders arrive continuously.

Customers

↓

Order Queue

↓

Order Processor

If orders arrive faster than they are processed:

  • Orders should wait safely.
  • Consumers should automatically process them when available.
  • Threads should not waste CPU by repeatedly checking for work.

docs.title: 15.2 What is a BlockingQueue?
docs.text:
A BlockingQueue is a thread-safe queue that automatically blocks producers or consumers when necessary.

It provides two key guarantees:

  • If the queue is full, producers wait.
  • If the queue is empty, consumers wait.

This removes the need for manual synchronization using wait() and notify().

Producer

↓

↓

The consumer processes tasks.

Neither side needs to know the speed of the other.

docs.title: 15.16 Spring Boot Example
docs.text:
@Service
public class OrderProcessor {

    private final BlockingQueue<Order> queue =
            new LinkedBlockingQueue<>();

    public void submit(Order order)
            throws InterruptedException {

        queue.put(order);

    }

    public void process()
            throws InterruptedException {

        while(true){

            Order order = queue.take();

            processOrder(order);

        }

    }

}

This pattern decouples order submission from order processing.

docs.text: It safely coordinates producers and consumers without manual synchronization.

docs.title: Q2. What happens when the queue is full?
docs.text:
• put() blocks.
  • offer() returns false.
  • Timed offer() waits for the specified duration.

docs.title: Q3. What happens when the queue is empty?
docs.text:
• take() blocks.
  • poll() returns null.
  • Timed poll() waits for the specified duration.

docs.title: Q4. Is BlockingQueue thread-safe?
docs.text:
Yes.

Its implementations are designed for concurrent producers and consumers.

docs.title: Q5. Where is BlockingQueue used?
docs.text:
• ThreadPoolExecutor

  • Kafka-style processing pipelines
  • Batch processing
  • Asynchronous services

docs.title: Production Scenario
docs.text:
Interviewer:

"Your payment gateway receives 20,000 payment requests per minute, but the payment processor can handle only 5,000 per minute. How would you design the system?"

A strong answer:

  • Place incoming requests into a bounded BlockingQueue.
  • Multiple worker threads consume requests from the queue.
  • A bounded queue provides back-pressure, preventing unbounded memory growth.
  • If the queue fills, decide on an appropriate strategy such as rejecting requests, retrying later, or scaling consumers.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
✅ Prefer bounded queues to avoid uncontrolled memory usage.

✅ Handle InterruptedException correctly by restoring the interrupt status.

✅ Choose the implementation that matches your workload.

✅ Monitor queue depth in production.

✅ Size worker threads based on CPU-bound vs I/O-bound workloads.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Using an unbounded queue without considering memory limits.

❌ Swallowing InterruptedException.

❌ Choosing PriorityBlockingQueue when FIFO ordering is required.

❌ Implementing busy-wait loops instead of using blocking methods.

docs.text:
• BlockingQueue is a thread-safe queue designed for producer-consumer coordination.
  • Producers block when the queue is full; consumers block when it is empty.
  • Different implementations address different requirements: bounded capacity, priority ordering, or delayed execution.
  • ThreadPoolExecutor relies heavily on BlockingQueue.
  • It is a foundational building block for scalable asynchronous Java applications.

docs.title: Chapter 17 - Atomic Classes & Compare-And-Swap (CAS)
docs.text:
"Locks provide correctness by making threads wait. Atomic classes achieve correctness by allowing threads to compete using hardware-supported atomic instructions. Instead of blocking, failed operations simply retry."

Atomic classes are the foundation of many high-performance concurrent data structures in Java, including ConcurrentHashMap, ConcurrentLinkedQueue, ForkJoinPool, and parts of the JVM itself.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After completing this chapter, you will understand:

  • Why Atomic Classes exist
  • Compare-And-Swap (CAS)
  • Hardware Atomic Instructions

docs.title: 17.1 Why Do We Need Atomic Classes?
docs.text:
Suppose multiple threads increment a counter.

count++;

Looks simple.

Internally it performs three operations.

Read

↓

Increment

↓

Write

These three operations are not atomic.

docs.title: 17.2 Race Condition
docs.text:
Initial value

count = 5

Thread A

Read = 5

Thread B

Read = 5

Thread A

Write = 6

Thread B

Write = 6

Expected

7

Actual

6

One update is lost.

docs.title: 17.3 Traditional Solution
docs.text:
Use synchronization.

synchronized void increment() {
    count++;
}

Problem:

Acquire Lock

↓

Increment

↓

Release Lock

Locks introduce:

  • Context switching
  • Waiting
  • Contention
  • Reduced throughput

Can we avoid locks?

Yes.

docs.title: 17.4 What is CAS?
docs.text:
CAS means

Compare-And-Swap

It is a single atomic CPU instruction.

Conceptually:

Current Value = 10

↓

Expected Value = 10 ?

↓

YES

↓

Replace with 11

↓

Success

If another thread already changed the value:

Current = 12

↓

Expected = 10

↓

NO

↓

Retry

No lock.

No waiting.

docs.title: 17.5 CAS Loop
docs.text:
Atomic operations internally use a retry loop.

Read Value

↓

Try CAS

↓

Success?

↓

YES → Done

↓

NO

↓

Read Again

↓

Retry

Only one thread succeeds each time.

docs.title: 17.6 AtomicInteger
docs.text:
Instead of

int count = 0;

use

AtomicInteger count =
    new AtomicInteger();

Increment

count.incrementAndGet();

No explicit synchronization required.

docs.title: 17.7 Example
docs.text:
AtomicInteger visitors =
    new AtomicInteger();

visitors.incrementAndGet();

System.out.println(
    visitors.get());

Output

1

docs.title: 17.8 Common AtomicInteger Methods
docs.text:
incrementAndGet();

Increment then return.

getAndIncrement();

Return current value,

then increment.

decrementAndGet();

Decrease value.

addAndGet(10);

Add a value atomically.

compareAndSet(old,new);

CAS operation.

docs.title: 17.9 compareAndSet()
docs.text:
Example

AtomicInteger balance =
    new AtomicInteger(100);

balance.compareAndSet(
    100,
    200);

Execution

Current = 100

↓

Expected = 100

↓

Update = 200

Returns

true

If another thread changed the balance first:

Returns

false

docs.title: 17.10 AtomicLong
docs.text:
Same concept.

AtomicLong requestCount =
    new AtomicLong();

Suitable for

  • API Counters
  • Metrics
  • Request Tracking

docs.title: 17.11 AtomicBoolean
docs.text:
Example

AtomicBoolean started =
    new AtomicBoolean(false);

Useful for

Application Started?

↓

YES

↓

Skip

Only one thread can successfully change the value from false to true using compareAndSet.

docs.title: 17.12 AtomicReference
docs.text:
Sometimes

objects

must be updated atomically.

AtomicReference<User> user =
    new AtomicReference<>();

Example

user.compareAndSet(
    oldUser,
    newUser);

Useful for immutable object replacement.

docs.title: 17.13 Production Example
docs.text:
Configuration Refresh

AtomicReference<Config> config =
    new AtomicReference<>();

Refresh

config.set(newConfig);

Readers

Config current =
    config.get();

No locking required for replacing the configuration reference.

docs.title: 17.14 Atomic Arrays
docs.text:
Java also provides

AtomicIntegerArray

AtomicLongArray

AtomicReferenceArray

Each element can be updated atomically.

Useful for:

  • Counters
  • Metrics
  • Shared state arrays

docs.title: 17.15 LongAdder
docs.text:
One of the most important interview topics.

Suppose

100 threads

increment

Counter

Using

AtomicInteger

All threads compete for one variable.

Contention increases.

LongAdder works differently.

Cell1

Cell2

Cell3

Cell4

Each thread updates a different internal cell.

Final value

Cell1

+

Cell2

+

Cell3

+

Cell4

Result:

Much higher throughput under heavy contention.

docs.title: 17.16 AtomicInteger vs LongAdder
docs.text:
Feature AtomicInteger LongAdder Single Variable ✅ ❌ (Multiple Cells) Low Contention Excellent Excellent High Contention Good Excellent Memory Usage Lower Higher

Use LongAdder for frequently updated shared counters.

docs.title: 17.17 ABA Problem
docs.text:
Classic CAS problem.

Suppose

Initial

A

Thread A

reads

A

Thread B changes

A

↓

B

↓

A

Thread A performs CAS.

CAS succeeds,

even though the value changed twice.

This is called the ABA Problem.

docs.title: 17.18 Solution to ABA
docs.text:
Java provides

AtomicStampedReference

Each value includes

Value

+

Version Number

Example

A,1

↓

B,2

↓

A,3

CAS detects the version change even though the value returned to A.

docs.title: 17.19 Real Spring Boot Example
docs.text:
API Request Counter

@Service
public class MetricsService {

    private final AtomicLong requests =
        new AtomicLong();

    public void increment() {

    requests.incrementAndGet();

    }

    public long totalRequests() {

    return requests.get();

    }

}

For very high request rates, consider LongAdder instead of AtomicLong.

docs.title: Q1. Why use AtomicInteger instead of synchronized?
docs.text: Atomic classes avoid blocking and generally perform better under low to moderate contention by using CAS instead of locks.

docs.title: Q2. What is CAS?
docs.text:
Compare-And-Swap.

An atomic operation that updates a value only if it still matches the expected value.

docs.title: Q3. Does CAS always succeed?
docs.text:
No.

If another thread updates the value first,

CAS fails,

and the operation retries or handles the failure.

docs.title: Q4. What is the ABA Problem?
docs.text:
A value changes from A → B → A.

A simple CAS cannot detect the intermediate modification.

docs.title: Q5. When should you use LongAdder?
docs.text: For high-contention counters where many threads frequently update the same value.

docs.title: Production Scenario
docs.text:
Interviewer:

"Your API gateway maintains a request counter that is incremented millions of times per minute. Which implementation would you choose?"

A strong answer:

  • AtomicLong is suitable for moderate contention.
  • Under very high contention, prefer LongAdder because it distributes updates across multiple internal cells, reducing contention.
  • If exact intermediate values are needed during updates, evaluate whether AtomicLong better matches the consistency requirements.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
✅ Use atomic classes for simple shared state.

✅ Use LongAdder for high-frequency counters.

✅ Use AtomicReference with immutable objects.

✅ Understand that CAS may retry under contention.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Replacing every lock with CAS.

❌ Assuming CAS always succeeds on the first attempt.

❌ Ignoring the ABA problem in advanced lock-free algorithms.

❌ Using AtomicInteger for highly contended metrics when LongAdder would scale better.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
• Atomic classes provide lock-free thread safety using CAS.
  • CAS compares the current value with an expected value before updating.
  • AtomicInteger, AtomicLong, AtomicBoolean, and AtomicReference support common atomic operations.
  • LongAdder improves scalability for highly contended counters.
  • The ABA problem can be addressed with versioned references such as AtomicStampedReference.

docs.title: Chapter 18: LongAdder & LongAccumulator
docs.text:
Interview Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (Senior Java Developer)

Asked In: Amazon, Oracle, Walmart, Visa, JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Microsoft, Flipkart, Adobe

docs.title: 1. Why Do Interviewers Ask This?
docs.text:
The interviewer is not checking whether you know the API.

They want to assess whether you understand:

  • High contention scenarios
  • Lock-free programming
  • CAS bottlenecks
  • JVM concurrent utilities
  • Performance optimization
  • Choosing the right data structure based on workload

Typical Interview Question:

We have an API receiving 200K requests/sec, and we need to maintain a request counter. Would you use AtomicLong or LongAdder? Why?

docs.title: 2. 30-Second Interview Answer
docs.text: AtomicLong stores the value in a single memory location. Every thread competes to update that location using CAS, which becomes a bottleneck under high contention. LongAdder distributes updates across multiple internal counters (cells), allowing different threads to update different cells concurrently. This significantly improves write throughput. The trade-off is that reading the value requires summing all cells, making reads slightly more expensive.

docs.title: 3. Interviewer's Expectation
docs.text:
After your 30-second answer, be prepared for:

  • Why does AtomicLong become slow?
  • What is CAS?
  • What are Cells?
  • What is Striped64?
  • How many Cells are created?
  • Is sum() atomic?
  • When should you NOT use LongAdder?

docs.title: 4. The Problem with AtomicLong
docs.text:
Imagine 10 threads incrementing the same counter.

AtomicLong

         +-------------+
Thread1 ----\
Thread2 -----\
Thread3 -------> Counter (100)
Thread4 -----/
Thread5 ----/
         +-------------+

Every thread tries to update one memory location.

Internally:

counter.incrementAndGet();

becomes

while(true){

   long current = value;

   long next = current + 1;

   if(compareAndSet(current,next))
       return;

}

If another thread modifies the value before CAS succeeds:

  • CAS fails
  • Retry
  • Retry
  • Retry

More contention → More retries → Lower throughput.

docs.title: 5. Production Scenario
docs.text:
Suppose you're building:

Payment Service

↓

Every payment increments

paymentsProcessed++

Traffic:

100 TPS

↓

500 TPS

↓

10,000 TPS

↓

200,000 TPS

With AtomicLong, every request competes for the same counter.

CPU spends more time retrying CAS than performing useful work.

docs.title: 6. Enter LongAdder
docs.text:
Instead of one counter:

Cell0

Cell1

Cell2

Cell3

Cell4

Threads spread across multiple cells.

Thread1 → Cell0

Thread2 → Cell1

Thread3 → Cell2

Thread4 → Cell3

Thread5 → Cell0

Each thread updates a different memory location.

Much less contention.

docs.title: 7. Internal Architecture
docs.text:
LongAdder
      │
      │
      ▼
+----------------------+
|      Striped64       |
+----------------------+
          │
          │
   +------+------+ 
   |             |
 base        Cell[]
               │
     +----+----+----+
     |    |    |    |
   Cell Cell Cell Cell

LongAdder extends Striped64, an internal JDK class that manages contention by dynamically creating multiple counters.

docs.title: 8. What is Striped64?
docs.text:
Striped64 is the foundation for:

  • LongAdder
  • LongAccumulator
  • DoubleAdder
  • DoubleAccumulator

It contains:

volatile long base;

volatile Cell[] cells;

Initially:

base = 0

cells = null

When contention is low:

Thread

↓

base++

Fast and memory-efficient.

docs.title: 9. What Happens Under Contention?
docs.text:
When CAS on base starts failing repeatedly:

CAS Failed

↓

Create Cell[]

↓

Distribute threads

↓

Retry

Example:

base

↓

CAS failure

↓

cells[2]

↓

cells[4]

↓

cells[1]

The JDK automatically expands the number of cells as contention increases.

docs.title: 10. How Does a Thread Pick a Cell?
docs.text:
Each thread has a pseudo-random probe value.

probe = 5

↓

5 % cells.length

↓

Cell5

Another thread:

probe = 12

↓

Cell4

This reduces the chance of multiple threads updating the same cell.

docs.title: 11. Dynamic Expansion
docs.text:
Suppose:

2 Cells

are not enough.

More contention occurs.

The JDK automatically expands:

2

↓

4

↓

8

↓

16

↓

32

Expansion stops when additional cells no longer improve throughput or when it reaches an implementation-defined limit (often related to available processors).

docs.title: 12. Reading the Value
docs.text:
Unlike AtomicLong:

counter.get();

LongAdder must compute:

base

+

Cell0

+

Cell1

+

Cell2

+

Cell3

Internally:

long total = base;

for(Cell c : cells){

    total += c.value;

}

Therefore:

Writes → Very Fast

Reads → Slightly Slower

docs.title: 13. Is sum() Atomic?
docs.text:
Interview favorite.

Answer: No.

Suppose:

Cell0 = 10

Cell1 = 20

While sum() is reading:

Thread

updates

Cell1 = 21

Possible result:

30

or

31

depending on timing.

For metrics and statistics, this is acceptable.

For banking balances, it is not.

docs.title: 14. When Should You Use LongAdder?
docs.text: Use Case LongAdder? Reason API Request Counter ✅ Heavy writes Prometheus Metrics ✅ Eventual accuracy is fine Kafka Consumer Metrics ✅ High throughput Login Counter ✅ Many increments Bank Balance ❌ Exact value required Inventory Stock ❌ Strong consistency required Wallet Balance ❌ Precise reads required

docs.title: 15. LongAccumulator
docs.text:
LongAccumulator generalizes LongAdder by allowing a custom accumulation function.

Example:

LongAccumulator maxAccumulator =
    new LongAccumulator(Long::max, Long.MIN_VALUE);

maxAccumulator.accumulate(120);
maxAccumulator.accumulate(250);
maxAccumulator.accumulate(180);

System.out.println(maxAccumulator.get()); // 250

Other examples include tracking minimum values or combining values with custom associative operations.

Use it when addition is not the operation you need.

docs.title: 16. LongAdder vs AtomicLong
docs.text: Feature AtomicLong LongAdder Updates Single variable Multiple cells Write Performance Good Excellent under contention Read Performance Excellent Good (needs aggregation) CAS Contention High Low Memory Usage Low Higher Best For Frequent reads Frequent writes

docs.title: Spring Boot Request Counter
docs.text:
@Component
public class ApiMetrics {

    private final LongAdder requestCounter = new LongAdder();

    public void increment() {
        requestCounter.increment();
    }

    public long getCount() {
        return requestCounter.sum();
    }
}

Every incoming request:

metrics.increment();

Periodic metrics export:

metrics.getCount();

This pattern is common in monitoring systems where write throughput is far more important than perfectly synchronized reads.

docs.title: ❓ Is LongAdder always better?
docs.text:
❌ No.

If reads are much more frequent than writes, AtomicLong may be a better choice because reads are just a single volatile access.

docs.title: ❓ Is LongAdder lock-free?
docs.text: ✅ Yes. It relies primarily on CAS and avoids traditional locks in normal operation.

docs.title: ❓ Does LongAdder guarantee perfectly consistent reads?
docs.text:
❌ No.

sum() provides a best-effort snapshot, not a transactional read.

docs.title: ❓ Why not synchronize everything?
docs.text: Locks serialize updates, reducing concurrency under heavy write loads.

docs.text:
1. Why does CAS fail under contention?
  2. What problem does Striped64 solve?
  3. How are cells allocated?
  4. Why is base still present?
  5. Why does sum() iterate over all cells?
  6. Is LongAdder linearizable?
  7. How does false sharing affect performance?
  8. When would AtomicLong outperform LongAdder?

  10. What is the difference between LongAdder and LongAccumulator?

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
• ✅ AtomicLong → Single memory location.
  • ✅ LongAdder → Multiple cells to reduce contention.
  • ✅ Built on Striped64.
  • ✅ Heavy writes → LongAdder.
  • ✅ Frequent reads with exact values → AtomicLong.
  • ✅ sum() is not an atomic snapshot.
  • ✅ Commonly used in metrics, monitoring, and high-throughput counters.

In the next chapter, we'll cover AtomicReference, AtomicStampedReference, and the ABA Problem, including how lock-free algorithms use CAS on object references, why the ABA problem occurs, and how the JDK solves it using version stamps-topics that frequently appear in senior backend interviews.

docs.title: Chapter 19: AtomicReference, AtomicStampedReference & the ABA Problem
docs.text:
Interview Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Senior/Lead Java Developer)

Frequently Asked By: Amazon, Microsoft, Oracle, Goldman Sachs, Visa, Walmart, Uber, Atlassian

docs.title: 1. Why Do Interviewers Ask This?
docs.text:
This topic separates mid-level developers from senior engineers.

The interviewer wants to know whether you understand:

  • Lock-free programming
  • CAS limitations
  • ABA Problem
  • JVM atomic primitives
  • Immutable object updates
  • Concurrent algorithm design

Typical question:

We know CAS prevents race conditions. Then why do we need AtomicStampedReference?

docs.title: 2. 30-Second Interview Answer
docs.text: AtomicReference atomically updates object references using CAS. However, CAS only checks whether the reference is the same-it cannot detect if the value changed from A→B→A in between. This is called the ABA problem. AtomicStampedReference solves it by associating a version number (stamp) with the reference, so CAS verifies both the object reference and its version.

docs.title: 3. Interviewer's Expectation
docs.text:
After the initial answer, expect:

  • What is AtomicReference?
  • Why not synchronized?
  • What is ABA?
  • Is ABA always a problem?
  • How does AtomicStampedReference work?
  • Difference between AtomicStampedReference and AtomicMarkableReference?
  • Where is ABA seen in production?

docs.title: 4. Why AtomicReference?
docs.text:
Atomic classes aren't limited to primitives.

Suppose:

class UserSession {
    String token;
    long expiry;
}

Two threads update the session.

Without synchronization:

session = new UserSession(...);

One update may overwrite another.

AtomicReference provides atomic replacement.

AtomicReference<UserSession> session =
    new AtomicReference<>();

docs.title: set()
docs.text:
session.set(newSession);

Blind replacement.

docs.title: get()
docs.text:
UserSession current = session.get();

Lock-free read.

docs.title: compareAndSet()
docs.text:
session.compareAndSet(oldSession, newSession);

Updates only if the current reference is exactly oldSession.

docs.title: 6. Production Example
docs.text:
Configuration Refresh

Imagine:

Current Config

↓

New Config arrives

↓

Replace entire object

Instead of modifying fields individually:

config.timeout = 30;
config.retry = 5;
config.url = "...";

Create a new immutable object:

Configuration newConfig =
    new Configuration(...);

configReference.set(newConfig);

Readers always see a consistent snapshot.

This pattern is common in:

  • Configuration management
  • Feature flags
  • Routing tables
  • Caches

docs.title: 7. CAS on Objects
docs.text:
Suppose

Reference

↓

User Object A

Thread A:

compareAndSet(A, B)

Works only if the reference still points to A.

CAS compares the reference, not the object's internal fields.

docs.title: 8. The ABA Problem
docs.text:
This is one of the most common senior interview questions.

Initial state:

Reference

↓

A

Thread 1 reads:

A

Before Thread 1 performs CAS...

Thread 2 executes:

A

↓

B

↓

A

Now Thread 1 performs:

compareAndSet(A, C)

CAS succeeds.

But something changed!

CAS couldn't detect:

A

↓

B

↓

A

This hidden modification is called the ABA Problem.

docs.title: 9. Why is ABA Dangerous?
docs.text:
Imagine a lock-free stack.

Initial:

Top

↓

Node A

↓

Node B

Thread 1 reads:

Top = A

Meanwhile

Thread 2:

  • Pops A
  • Pops B
  • Pushes A again

Stack becomes

Top

↓

A

Thread 1 still thinks nothing changed.

CAS succeeds.

The stack is now corrupted.

docs.title: 10. Real Production Example
docs.text:
Memory allocators

Network packet queues

Lock-free stacks

Work-stealing schedulers

These algorithms reuse objects.

Reference may become:

A

↓

B

↓

A

CAS cannot distinguish this.

docs.title: 11. AtomicStampedReference
docs.text:
Solution:

Store

Reference

+

Version Number

Instead of

A

Store

(A,1)

Update:

(B,2)

Again:

(A,3)

Even though reference returned to A,

Version changed.

CAS fails correctly.

docs.title: 12. Internal View
docs.text:
Instead of

Reference

↓

Object

Store

Reference

↓

Object

Stamp = 5

CAS checks

Reference

AND

Stamp

Both must match.

docs.title: 13. Example
docs.text:
AtomicStampedReference<String> ref =
    new AtomicStampedReference<>("A",1);

Current

(A,1)

Update

int stamp = ref.getStamp();

ref.compareAndSet(
    "A",
    "B",
    stamp,
    stamp+1
);

Result

(B,2)

docs.title: 14. ABA Detection
docs.text:
Thread1 reads

(A,1)

Thread2

(A,1)

↓

(B,2)

↓

(A,3)

Thread1

tries

CAS(A,1)

Fails.

Why?

Current value

(A,3)

Stamp changed.

Exactly what we wanted.

docs.title: 15. AtomicMarkableReference
docs.text:
Instead of

Reference + Version

Stores

Reference + Boolean

Reference

Deleted = true

Useful for:

  • Logical deletion
  • Lock-free linked lists
  • Concurrent skip lists

Not useful when version history matters.

docs.title: 16. Comparison
docs.text: Feature AtomicReference AtomicStampedReference AtomicMarkableReference Atomic Object Update ✅ ✅ ✅ Version Tracking ❌ ✅ ❌ Boolean Marker ❌ ❌ ✅ Solves ABA ❌ ✅ Partially Memory Overhead Low Higher Medium

docs.title: 17. Immutable Object Pattern
docs.text:
One of the best production practices.

Instead of

config.setUrl(...);
config.setRetry(...);
config.setTimeout(...);

Do

Configuration updated =
    new Configuration(...);

configRef.set(updated);

Benefits

  • Thread-safe
  • No partial updates
  • Easy rollback
  • Easy caching

docs.title: Is AtomicReference thread-safe?
docs.text:
✅ Yes.

Updating the reference is atomic.

The object it points to may still be mutable and require its own synchronization.

docs.title: Does AtomicReference solve every concurrency issue?
docs.text:
❌ No.

Only the reference update is atomic.

docs.title: Does AtomicStampedReference eliminate ABA?
docs.text: ✅ It detects ABA by including a version stamp.

docs.title: Why not always use AtomicStampedReference?
docs.text: Extra memory and version management introduce overhead. If ABA is impossible or irrelevant, AtomicReference is simpler and faster.

docs.title: 19. Senior-Level Follow-up Questions
docs.text:
1. What exactly does CAS compare for object references?
  2. Why can't CAS detect ABA?
  3. Where does ABA occur in production?
  4. Why is AtomicStampedReference slower?
  5. Why does AtomicReference work well with immutable objects?
  6. How does ConcurrentLinkedQueue avoid corruption?
  7. Why are lock-free algorithms difficult to implement?
  8. Is AtomicReference linearizable?
  9. What is AtomicMarkableReference used for?
  10. Why doesn't every concurrent collection use AtomicStampedReference?

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: A high-throughput lock-free queue occasionally loses elements under stress testing.

docs.title: Investigation
docs.text:
• No locks
  • Heavy CAS retries
  • Objects recycled frequently

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text: ABA caused a CAS operation to succeed even though the node had been removed and reinserted.

docs.title: Fix
docs.text:
• Introduce versioned references (AtomicStampedReference) where appropriate, or redesign the algorithm to avoid node reuse without safe reclamation.
  • Re-test with high-concurrency stress tests (for example, jcstress or similar concurrency testing approaches).

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
• ✅ AtomicReference performs atomic updates on object references.
  • ✅ CAS checks the reference value, not the object's internal state.
  • ✅ ABA means a value changes A → B → A, making a simple CAS believe nothing changed.
  • ✅ AtomicStampedReference pairs the reference with a version number to detect ABA.
  • ✅ AtomicMarkableReference pairs a reference with a boolean flag, useful for logical deletion.
  • ✅ Prefer immutable objects with AtomicReference for configuration, caches, routing tables, and feature flags.

docs.title: Chapter 20: Lock-Free Programming Patterns
docs.text:
Interview Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Senior/Lead Java Engineer)

Frequently Asked By: Amazon, Microsoft, Oracle, Goldman Sachs, Uber, Atlassian, Visa, Walmart

docs.title: 1. Why Do Interviewers Ask This?
docs.text:
This topic tests whether you think like a systems engineer, not just a Java developer.

The interviewer wants to know if you understand:

  • High-performance concurrent systems
  • Lock-free algorithms
  • CPU architecture
  • JVM internals
  • Performance trade-offs
  • Designing scalable backend services

Typical question:

Why do high-performance systems like Kafka and Disruptor avoid locks?

docs.title: 2. 30-Second Interview Answer
docs.text: Lock-free programming uses atomic operations like CAS instead of locks to coordinate multiple threads. Unlike locks, threads don't block each other, reducing context switching and improving scalability. However, lock-free algorithms are harder to design because they must handle retries, ABA problems, memory ordering, and contention correctly.

docs.title: 3. The Problem with Locks
docs.text:
Imagine 20 threads updating a shared queue.

               Queue

                 ▲
                 │
        ReentrantLock
                 │
 ─────────────────────────────
 T1 Waiting
 T2 Waiting
 T3 Waiting
 ...
 T20 Waiting

Only one thread can proceed.

Problems:

  • Context switching
  • Thread parking/unparking
  • CPU idle time
  • Lower throughput
  • Lock contention

docs.title: 4. What is Lock-Free Programming?
docs.text:
Instead of waiting:

lock.lock();
try {
    counter++;
} finally {
    lock.unlock();
}

Threads continuously attempt an atomic operation.

while (true) {

    int current = value.get();

    int next = current + 1;

    if (value.compareAndSet(current, next))
        break;
}

If CAS fails:

  • Retry immediately
  • No blocking
  • No sleeping
  • No OS scheduler involvement

docs.title: 5. Progress Guarantees
docs.text:
One of the favorite senior interview topics.

Technique Progress Guarantee Example Blocking No synchronized Lock-Free At least one thread progresses ConcurrentLinkedQueue Wait-Free Every thread progresses Specialized algorithms Obstruction-Free Progress only without interference Rare algorithms

↓

Thread B

WAITING

docs.title: Lock-Free
docs.text:

docs.text:
Thread A ✓

Thread B ✓

Thread C ✓

Every thread finishes within a finite number of steps.

Extremely difficult to implement.

Rare in enterprise Java.

docs.title: Obstruction-Free
docs.text:
Works only if a thread eventually executes without contention.

Least practical.

docs.title: 6. Lock-Free vs Wait-Free
docs.text:
Feature Lock-Free Wait-Free Some thread always progresses ✅ ✅ Every thread progresses ❌ ✅ Complexity Medium Very High Used in Java Collections Yes Rarely

Interview Tip:

ConcurrentLinkedQueue is lock-free, not wait-free.

docs.title: 7. CAS Retry Loop
docs.text:
Every lock-free algorithm depends on this pattern.

while (true) {

    State old = ref.get();

    State updated = modify(old);

    if (ref.compareAndSet(old, updated))
        break;
}

Flow:

Read

↓

Modify

↓

CAS

↓

Success?

↓

Yes → Done

↓

No → Retry

docs.title: 16. Kafka and Lock-Free Concepts
docs.text:
Interview Question:

Is Kafka completely lock-free?

Answer: No.

Kafka uses synchronization in several components, but many performance-critical paths are designed to minimize locking.

Examples:

  • Sequential append to logs
  • Efficient batching
  • Atomic variables
  • Optimized concurrent data structures

Interview Tip:

Don't claim Kafka is "100% lock-free." A more accurate statement is:

"Kafka minimizes locking on hot paths and combines lock-free techniques with carefully designed synchronization where required."

docs.title: Is lock-free always faster?
docs.text:
❌ No.

For low contention,

a simple synchronized block may be faster and much easier to maintain.

docs.title: Is CAS free?
docs.text:
❌ No.

CAS is an expensive CPU instruction.

Repeated failures waste CPU cycles.

docs.title: Can lock-free algorithms starve threads?
docs.text:
✅ Yes.

A thread can continuously lose CAS races while others keep succeeding.

docs.title: Why not replace every lock with CAS?
docs.text: Complex algorithms become much harder to reason about and maintain. Sometimes a well-designed lock is simpler and performs adequately.

docs.text:

docs.title: Expected Answer
docs.text:

  • LongAdder is the preferred choice for metrics or counters where slightly stale reads are acceptable.
  • If the value represents money or account balances requiring strict consistency, neither is sufficient by itself-you'd need a design that guarantees correctness, potentially involving locks, transactional updates, or database concurrency controls depending on the architecture.

This shows you understand both performance and correctness, which is what interviewers look for.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• ✅ Lock-free algorithms rely on CAS, not locks.
  • ✅ They reduce blocking but increase implementation complexity.
  • ✅ Lock-free ≠ Wait-free.
  • ✅ False sharing can significantly reduce performance.
  • ✅ Cache-friendly data structures often outperform theoretically optimal ones.
  • ✅ Choose the right tool based on contention, correctness, latency, and maintainability, not just raw performance.

docs.title: Part V - Executor Framework & Asynchronous Programming
Chapter 21: Executor Framework & ExecutorService
docs.text:
Interview Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Asked in: Amazon, Microsoft, Oracle, Goldman Sachs, Walmart, Visa, Adobe, Atlassian

docs.title: 1. Why Do Interviewers Ask This?
docs.text:
This topic reveals whether you understand how Java applications execute tasks in production.

The interviewer wants to assess whether you understand:

  • Why manually creating threads is a bad idea
  • Thread lifecycle
  • Thread pooling
  • Resource management
  • Scalability
  • Task execution
  • Production best practices

Typical interview question:

Why should we use ExecutorService instead of creating threads using new Thread()?

docs.title: 2. 30-Second Interview Answer
docs.text: Creating a new thread for every task is expensive because thread creation, scheduling, and destruction consume CPU and memory. ExecutorService manages a pool of reusable worker threads, reducing thread creation overhead, controlling concurrency, improving throughput, and providing lifecycle management such as graceful shutdown.

docs.title: 3. The Problem with new Thread()
docs.text:
Junior developers often write:

new Thread(() -> processOrder()).start();

Looks simple.

But imagine your REST API receives:

20 requests/sec

No problem.

Now imagine:

10,000 requests/sec

Now you're creating

10,000 Threads

Problems:

  • Huge memory consumption
  • CPU context switching
  • Thread scheduling overhead
  • Thread creation cost
  • Possible OutOfMemoryError

docs.title: 4. Why is Thread Creation Expensive?
docs.text:
A Java thread is not just a Java object.

Creating a thread involves:

Application

↓

JVM

↓

Native Thread

↓

Operating System

↓

Kernel

↓

CPU Scheduler

Each thread requires:

  • Native OS thread
  • Thread stack (typically 1 MB by default, JVM/OS dependent)
  • Scheduling metadata
  • Context-switch support

Creating thousands of threads is costly.

docs.title: 5. Production Scenario
docs.text:
Imagine a payment service.

Every payment triggers:

new Thread(() -> sendEmail()).start();

Traffic:

50 TPS

↓

500 TPS

↓

5000 TPS

Soon:

  • Thousands of live threads
  • High CPU utilization
  • Increased GC pressure
  • Slow response times

docs.title: 6. The Executor Framework
docs.text:
Instead of creating threads,

submit tasks.

Application

↓

ExecutorService

↓

Task Queue

↓

Worker Threads

↓

Execution

The application no longer manages threads directly.

It delegates thread management to the framework.

docs.title: 7. Core Interfaces
docs.text:
Executor
        │
        ▼
ExecutorService
        │
        ▼
ScheduledExecutorService

docs.title: Executor
docs.text:
Simple interface.

public interface Executor {

    void execute(Runnable command);

}

Only executes tasks.

No shutdown.

No result.

docs.title: ExecutorService
docs.text:
Adds:

  • submit()
  • Future
  • shutdown()
  • invokeAll()
  • invokeAny()

docs.title: ScheduledExecutorService
docs.text:
Adds scheduling support.

  • Delayed execution
  • Fixed-rate execution
  • Fixed-delay execution

docs.title: 8. Creating an ExecutorService
docs.text:
ExecutorService executor =
        Executors.newFixedThreadPool(5);

Five worker threads are created.

Suppose you submit 100 tasks.

100 Tasks

↓

Queue

↓

5 Threads

↓

Execution

Only five tasks execute concurrently.

The remaining tasks wait in the queue.

docs.title: execute()
docs.text:
executor.execute(() -> processOrder());

Characteristics:

  • No return value
  • Exceptions go to the thread's uncaught exception handler

docs.title: submit()
docs.text:
Future<String> future =
        executor.submit(() -> processOrder());

Characteristics:

  • Returns a Future
  • Exceptions are captured and rethrown when calling future.get()

Interview Question

Which one do you prefer?

Answer:

  • Use execute() for fire-and-forget tasks.
  • Use submit() when you need a result or exception handling through Future.

docs.title: Runnable
docs.text:
Runnable task = () -> {

    processOrder();

};

Returns

void

Cannot throw checked exceptions directly.

docs.title: Callable
docs.text:
Callable<Order> task = () -> {

    return processOrder();

};

Returns

Order

Can throw checked exceptions.

docs.title: 11. Future
docs.text:
Future represents the result of an asynchronous computation.

Future<String> future =
        executor.submit(() -> "SUCCESS");

Later:

String result = future.get();

Important:

future.get() blocks until the task completes.

docs.title: 12. Production Example
docs.text:
Invoice generation.

REST Request

↓

Submit Task

↓

ExecutorService

↓

Generate PDF

↓

Store in S3

↓

Return Download Link

The REST thread is freed quickly while background processing continues.

docs.title: 13. Executor Lifecycle
docs.text:
Many candidates forget this.

Created

↓

Running

↓

Shutdown Requested

↓

No New Tasks

↓

Existing Tasks Complete

↓

Terminated

docs.title: shutdown()
docs.text:
executor.shutdown();
  • Stops accepting new tasks
  • Allows queued/running tasks to finish

docs.title: shutdownNow()
docs.text:
executor.shutdownNow();
  • Attempts to interrupt running tasks
  • Returns tasks that never started
  • Interruption is cooperative-tasks must respond to interrupts

Interview Trap

Does shutdownNow() always stop every thread immediately?

No.

A task that ignores interruption may continue running.

docs.title: 15. Production Best Practices
docs.text:
✅ Prefer dependency-injected executors (for example, in Spring) instead of creating executors throughout the codebase.

✅ Always shut down executors you create manually.

✅ Give worker threads meaningful names.

✅ Monitor queue size and active thread count.

❌ Never create a new executor for every request.

❌ Never use Executors factory methods blindly in production without understanding their queueing behavior.

docs.title: Is ExecutorService a thread?
docs.text:
❌ No.

It manages a collection of worker threads.

docs.title: Does submit() create a new thread?
docs.text:
❌ No.

It submits a task.

The pool decides which worker executes it.

docs.title: Can one thread execute multiple tasks?
docs.text:
✅ Yes.

Worker threads are reused.

docs.title: Is Future asynchronous?
docs.text:
Not by itself.

The task executes asynchronously, but Future.get() is a blocking call.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: A Spring Boot application gradually slows down after several days.

docs.title: Investigation
docs.text:
• Heap looks normal
  • Database is healthy
  • CPU is moderate
  • Thousands of threads remain active

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text:
Developers created new executors repeatedly:

public void sendEmail() {

    ExecutorService executor =
        Executors.newFixedThreadPool(5);

    executor.submit(...);

}

Each invocation creates a new thread pool that is never shut down.

docs.title: Fix
docs.text:
• Create a shared executor.
  • Reuse it across the application.
  • Shut it down gracefully during application shutdown.

Chapter 22: ThreadPoolExecutor Internals (The Most Important Concurrency Topic)
docs.text:
Interview Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Frequently Asked In: Amazon, Microsoft, Oracle, Goldman Sachs, Visa, Walmart, Adobe, Atlassian

docs.title: 1. Why Do Interviewers Ask This?
docs.text:
This is one of the highest-value topics in Senior Java interviews.

The interviewer isn't checking whether you've used:

Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10);

They want to know if you understand:

  • How thread pools work internally
  • How tasks are scheduled
  • How queues affect throughput
  • Why applications become slow
  • How to tune thread pools
  • How to debug production issues

Typical interview question:

Explain what happens internally when I call executor.submit(task)

If you can answer that confidently, you're already ahead of many candidates.

docs.title: 2. 30-Second Interview Answer
docs.text: ThreadPoolExecutor manages a pool of reusable worker threads. When a task is submitted, it first tries to use an idle core thread. If all core threads are busy, the task is queued. If the queue is full and the pool hasn't reached its maximum size, new threads are created. Once both the queue and maximum threads are exhausted, the task is rejected using the configured rejection policy.

docs.title: 3. The Architecture
docs.text:
submit()

                  │
                  ▼

           ThreadPoolExecutor

       ┌──────────┬──────────┐
       │          │          │
       ▼          ▼          ▼

  Core Threads   Task Queue  Extra Threads

                  │

                  ▼

            Worker Threads

                  │

                  ▼

             Execute Task

Think of ThreadPoolExecutor as a manager.

It decides:

  • Should an existing thread execute?
  • Should I queue the task?
  • Should I create another thread?
  • Should I reject the task?

docs.text:

    int corePoolSize,

)

↓

5

If fewer than 5 threads exist,

new tasks immediately create new workers.

Example

Task1

↓

Thread1

Thread2

...

Task5

docs.text: One of the highest-value interview topics.

Task1

docs.title: 14. Rejection Policies
docs.text:
Suppose

Everything is full.

What happens?

The executor invokes a RejectedExecutionHandler.

docs.title: AbortPolicy
docs.text:
Default.

Throws

RejectedExecutionException

Application Thread

↓

docs.text:

docs.text:

docs.title: CPU-bound
docs.text:
Examples

  • Encryption
  • Image Processing
  • JSON Parsing

Recommended size

Number of CPU cores
or
CPU cores + 1

Reason

Extra threads mostly increase context switching.

docs.title: IO-bound
docs.text:
Examples

  • Database
  • HTTP Calls
  • Kafka
  • Redis

Since threads spend time waiting,

you can use more threads than CPU cores.

A common starting point is to size the pool based on expected wait time vs compute time, then measure and tune under production-like load rather than relying on a fixed formula.

@Configuration
public class ExecutorConfig {

    @Bean
    public ThreadPoolTaskExecutor orderExecutor() {

       ThreadPoolTaskExecutor executor =
             new ThreadPoolTaskExecutor();

       executor.setCorePoolSize(10);
       executor.setMaxPoolSize(30);
       executor.setQueueCapacity(200);
       executor.setThreadNamePrefix("order-");

       executor.initialize();

       return executor;
    }

}

Then

@Async("orderExecutor")
public void processOrder() {

}

This is a much better practice than relying on Spring Boot's default executor for every asynchronous task.

docs.text:

Too many threads increase context switching, memory usage, and scheduler overhead.

docs.text:
❌ No.

Threads are created lazily as tasks arrive, up to the core pool size.

docs.title: Why shouldn't I always use CachedThreadPool?
docs.text: Because it can create a very large number of threads if tasks arrive faster than they complete, potentially exhausting system resources.

docs.title: Why is a huge queue dangerous?
docs.text: It can hide overload by letting requests pile up, increasing latency and memory usage instead of applying back-pressure.

docs.title: 1. Why Do Interviewers Ask This?
docs.text:
Most developers have used ForkJoinPool indirectly.

Very few understand how it works.

Interviewers ask this topic to evaluate whether you understand:

  • Parallel computation
  • CPU utilization
  • Work-Stealing
  • Divide & Conquer algorithms

  • CompletableFuture internals

Typical Interview Question:

What is ForkJoinPool? Why doesn't it use a single task queue like ThreadPoolExecutor?

docs.title: 2. 30-Second Interview Answer
docs.text: ForkJoinPool is a specialized thread pool optimized for CPU-bound divide-and-conquer tasks. Instead of using a single shared queue, every worker thread maintains its own deque (double-ended queue). Idle workers steal tasks from busy workers, improving CPU utilization and reducing contention. It powers Parallel Streams and, by default, many CompletableFuture asynchronous operations.

docs.title: 3. Why ThreadPoolExecutor Isn't Always Enough
docs.text:
Suppose we need to process

10 Million Records

Using ThreadPoolExecutor:

Task

↓

Queue

↓

Worker Thread

One queue.

Problem:

One worker gets a huge task.

Others finish early.

Thread1 → Busy

Thread2 → Idle

Thread3 → Idle

Thread4 → Idle

Poor CPU utilization.

docs.title: 4. The Divide and Conquer Idea
docs.text:
Instead of processing

10 Million Records

Split them.

10M

↓

5M + 5M

↓

2.5M + 2.5M + 2.5M + 2.5M

↓

...

↓

Small Tasks

Every CPU core gets work.

docs.text:
ForkJoinPool

      ▼          ▼          ▼

 Worker1     Worker2     Worker3

    │            │            │

Deque1      Deque2      Deque3

Each worker owns its own queue.

This is the key difference from ThreadPoolExecutor.

docs.text:
Deque = Double Ended Queue

Front

↓

Task1

Task2

Task3

↓

Back

Owner thread:

  • Pushes tasks
  • Pops tasks

Idle threads:

  • Steal from opposite end

This minimizes contention.

docs.title: Strong Answer
docs.text: parallelStream() isn't always faster. If the workload is small, the overhead of splitting tasks and combining results can outweigh the benefits. If the work is I/O-bound, ForkJoinPool threads spend time blocked, reducing throughput. If the common pool is already busy with other tasks, contention can also hurt performance. I'd first profile the application before deciding whether parallel execution is appropriate.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• ✅ ForkJoinPool is optimized for CPU-bound workloads.
  • ✅ Each worker has its own deque, reducing contention.
  • ✅ Work-stealing keeps CPU cores busy by balancing work dynamically.
  • ✅ parallelStream() and the default CompletableFuture.supplyAsync() use the common ForkJoinPool unless another executor is supplied.
  • ✅ Avoid using the common pool for blocking I/O tasks.

"I avoid blindly using parallelStream() in production. Before choosing it, I evaluate whether the workload is CPU-bound or I/O-bound, the size of the data set, and whether using the shared ForkJoinPool.commonPool() could interfere with other parts of the application. For blocking workloads, I prefer a dedicated ExecutorService."

That answer demonstrates not just API knowledge, but engineering judgment-the quality interviewers are looking for.

docs.text: ScheduledExecutorService schedules tasks using a thread pool, unlike Timer which relies on a single thread. scheduleAtFixedRate() attempts to maintain a fixed schedule based on the initial start time, whereas scheduleWithFixedDelay() waits for one execution to finish before waiting the configured delay. Fixed-rate is suitable for periodic tasks like metrics collection, while fixed-delay is safer for long-running jobs.

  • One uncaught exception terminates the timer thread

Interview Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Frequently Asked In: Amazon, Oracle, Microsoft, Goldman Sachs, Uber, Atlassian, VMware, Modern Java 21 Interviews

docs.title: 1. Why Do Interviewers Ask This?
docs.text:
Virtual Threads are the biggest change to Java concurrency since the Executor Framework.

If you're interviewing for Java 21+, expect questions like:

  • What are Virtual Threads?
  • Why were they introduced?
  • How are they different from platform threads?
  • Do they replace thread pools?
  • What is thread pinning?
  • Can I migrate existing Spring Boot applications?

docs.title: 2. 30-Second Interview Answer
docs.text: Virtual Threads are lightweight threads introduced in Java 21. Unlike platform threads, they are managed primarily by the JVM instead of being permanently tied to an operating system thread. A virtual thread occupies a platform (carrier) thread only while it is actively running. When it blocks on supported operations such as network I/O, the JVM unmounts it so the carrier thread can execute other virtual threads. This enables applications to handle very large numbers of concurrent tasks using the familiar thread-per-request programming model.

docs.title: 3. The Problem Before Virtual Threads
docs.text:
Traditional Java

new Thread(() -> processRequest()).start();

Every Java thread

↓

One OS Thread

Java Thread 1
      │
      ▼
 OS Thread 1

Java Thread 2
      │
      ▼
 OS Thread 2

10,000 requests

↓

10,000 OS Threads

Problems

  • Huge memory usage
  • Context switching
  • Scheduler overhead
  • Poor scalability

docs.text:
Traditional threads are now called

Platform Threads

Relationship

1 Java Thread

↓

1 OS Thread

Expensive.

docs.title: 5. Virtual Threads

Running on

Possible because

Virtual Threads

≠

OS Threads

docs.text:

             │

             │

             ▼

      Carrier Threads

        PT1   PT2   PT3

             │

             ▼

         Operating System

The JVM schedules virtual threads onto a smaller set of carrier (platform) threads.

docs.text:

thread.start();

Each submitted task gets its own virtual thread.

docs.text:
Examples include:

synchronized(lock) {

    callDatabase();

}

If the thread blocks while inside a synchronized section,

Other examples:

  • Native/JNI calls
  • Some blocking operations that cannot be cooperatively managed

docs.text:
Instead of

}

ReentrantLock is generally a better fit for code that may block while running on virtual threads, although the best choice still depends on your concurrency requirements.

docs.title: 15. Where Virtual Threads Shine
docs.text:
Excellent for

  • REST APIs
  • Database calls
  • HTTP clients
  • Kafka consumers
  • File I/O
  • Messaging
  • Microservices

Why?

Because these workloads spend much of their time waiting.

docs.title: 16. Where They Don't Help Much
docs.text:
CPU-intensive tasks

Examples

  • Encryption
  • Image Processing
  • Video Encoding
  • AI Model Training

These tasks keep the CPU busy rather than waiting.

Adding millions of virtual threads won't make the CPU execute faster.

Each blocking call can execute in its own virtual thread, making the code look synchronous while still scaling well for I/O-bound workloads.

docs.title: Do Virtual Threads replace CompletableFuture?
docs.text:
❌ No.

They solve different problems.

  • Virtual Threads simplify thread management.
  • CompletableFuture simplifies asynchronous composition and combining results.

Often they complement each other.

docs.title: Do Virtual Threads replace ThreadPoolExecutor?
docs.text:
Not entirely.

They replace many thread-pool use cases centred on thread reuse.

You may still need executors to:

  • Limit concurrency
  • Prioritise tasks
  • Schedule work
  • Isolate workloads

docs.title: Are Virtual Threads faster?
docs.text:
Not necessarily.

They are more scalable for blocking workloads, not inherently faster for CPU-bound computation.

docs.title: Can I create one million Virtual Threads?
docs.text:
Potentially yes, depending on available memory and workload characteristics.

That does not mean one million tasks will execute simultaneously.

docs.title: Strong Answer

I'd still ensure that downstream resources such as database connection pools and HTTP client limits are configured appropriately, because Virtual Threads don't remove those bottlenecks.

✅ Avoid holding locks while performing long blocking operations.

docs.title: ⭐ Interview Secret
docs.text:
When an interviewer asks:

"Should every Java 21 application switch to Virtual Threads?"

A strong senior answer is:

"Not automatically. I'd first identify whether the application is I/O-bound or CPU-bound. Virtual Threads provide the biggest benefit for blocking operations such as database access and HTTP calls. For CPU-intensive workloads, they don't improve throughput. I'd also validate library compatibility, watch for thread pinning, and ensure downstream resources like connection pools are tuned appropriately."

This demonstrates balanced engineering judgement rather than treating Virtual Threads as a universal solution.

docs.title: 1. Why Do Interviewers Ask This?
docs.text:
This is one of the first JVM questions asked in senior Java interviews.

The interviewer wants to know whether you understand:

  • How Java applications execute
  • Where objects are stored
  • Where local variables live
  • How methods are executed
  • Why StackOverflowError occurs
  • Why OutOfMemoryError occurs

Typical interview question:

Explain JVM Memory Areas.

docs.title: 2. 30-Second Interview Answer
docs.text: The JVM divides memory into several runtime areas. The Heap stores objects and is shared by all threads. Each thread has its own Stack, which stores method frames, local variables, and references. The Program Counter (PC) Register keeps track of the next instruction to execute. The Native Method Stack supports JNI/native code. The Method Area stores class metadata and, in modern JVMs, is implemented using Metaspace.

docs.text:
The Heap stores:

  • Objects
  • Arrays
  • Object instances

Example

Student student = new Student();

Memory

Stack                  Heap

student ─────────────► Student Object

Important:

The variable is not stored in the Heap.

Only the object is.

docs.text:
Every thread gets its own stack.

The stack stores:

  • Local variables
  • Primitive values
  • Object references
  • Method call frames

Example

public void calculate() {

    int x = 10;

    Student s = new Student();

}

Memory

Stack Frame

docs.text:

its frame is removed.

docs.text:
Each thread has its own PC Register.

Purpose

Tracks

Next JVM Instruction

Without it,

the JVM couldn't resume execution correctly after context switches.

docs.text:
Used for

  • JNI

Example

❌ Generally no.

Objects are typically allocated on the heap. However, modern JVMs may optimise some allocations (for example, through escape analysis and scalar replacement), but this is an implementation optimisation and shouldn't change your conceptual model.

Error

Investigation

Application repeatedly created new class loaders for dynamically generated classes without releasing them.

Result

Metaspace kept growing.

Fix

  • Eliminate the class loader leak.
  • Reuse class loaders where appropriate.
  • Set monitoring and sensible Metaspace limits.

docs.title: 1. Why Do Interviewers Ask This?
docs.text:
Garbage Collection (GC) is one of the most frequently discussed JVM topics in senior Java interviews.

The interviewer wants to evaluate whether you understand:

  • How the JVM reclaims memory
  • Why memory leaks still occur in Java
  • Object lifecycle
  • Young vs Old Generation
  • Minor, Major, and Full GC
  • Object promotion
  • Performance implications

Typical interview question:

Explain how Garbage Collection works in Java.

docs.title: 2. 30-Second Interview Answer
docs.text: Java uses Garbage Collection (GC) to automatically reclaim memory occupied by objects that are no longer reachable. The JVM identifies live objects starting from GC Roots using reachability analysis. Most new objects are allocated in the Young Generation and reclaimed during Minor GC. Objects that survive multiple collections are promoted to the Old Generation, where they are collected less frequently because they are expected to live longer.

After the method finishes:

I'd analyse GC logs and inspect a heap dump with tools like Eclipse MAT or VisualVM to identify the dominant retained objects and reference chains.

When the interviewer asks:

"Why is Java Garbage Collection efficient?"

A senior-level answer is:

"The JVM is based on the Generational Hypothesis that most objects die young. By focusing frequent collections on the Young Generation, where short-lived objects are created, the JVM avoids repeatedly scanning long-lived objects in the Old Generation. This significantly reduces GC overhead for typical enterprise applications."

Most senior Java interviews eventually include questions like:

  • Why G1 instead of Parallel GC?

Which Garbage Collector would you choose for a Java 21 Spring Boot application and why?

docs.title: 2. 30-Second Interview Answer
docs.text: Modern JVMs provide multiple garbage collectors optimized for different workloads. Parallel GC maximizes throughput, G1 GC balances throughput with predictable pause times and is the default in modern JDKs, while ZGC and Shenandoah focus on extremely low pause times for very large heaps. The right choice depends on the application's latency, throughput, heap size, and SLA requirements.

docs.text:
When an interviewer asks:

"Which GC should we use?"

Avoid giving a one-word answer like:

"Use G1."

A senior-level answer is:

"The choice depends on business requirements. If throughput is the priority, Parallel GC may be appropriate. For most server applications, G1 is a strong default because it balances throughput and pause times. If the application has very large heaps and strict latency SLAs, I'd evaluate ZGC or Shenandoah. Before switching collectors, I'd always analyse GC logs and profile the application because the collector isn't always the root cause of performance problems."

That demonstrates an understanding of trade-offs, performance engineering, and production diagnostics rather than memorising JVM options.
